format: {name, note, act: {kind, args}, request: {method, path, ownerKey, token?, protocol, body}, response: {status, body}, outcome, binds?}. The cases run in order against one fresh Pond (the Telegram fake, a pinned clock). Asks, keys and session acts a case does not show were made through the Pond's own API before the first case, unless a case's note says they happened since. `act` is what the phone was asked to do; `request` is exactly what it sends: `ownerKey` true sends the approved X-Hook-Owner-Key, false none, "unknown" a key the Pond never approved; `token` "wrong" sends a wrong Pond token (absent: the right one); `protocol` is the X-Hook-Protocol sent. `outcome` maps the response: 2xx ok, 401 unauthorized, 404 notFound, 403 "owner key required" ownerKeyRequired, 403 "unknown owner key" ownerKeyRefused, 409 "ask was corrected" corrected, 409 "requirements_unmet" requirementsUnmet, 409 "ask is closed" askClosed, 409 "too many messages" tooManyMessages, any other 4xx invalid. `binds` names an id the response carries ({"ask1": "items.0.id"}, a number indexes a list); later paths and args use it as {ask1}. In responses every bound id is its {name} and every ISO-8601 timestamp is {time}, except a revision's `at`, kept as recorded because its hash covers it. `rev` and `hash` in a request body and in act.args are the real values the Pond accepts.
